me-1.question: Who are you? (The real story)
me-1.answer: I am a technologist passionate about leveraging modern tools to create impactful solutions. My journey started small—with a simple Python chatbot—but quickly grew into a fascination with modern AI, Large Language Models, and the intersection of industry engineering and HCI research. I bring a 'builder's mindset' to my work, inspired by my childhood favorites: LEGO and Transformers. I was always mesmerized by how small LEGO bricks could join to form a complex structure, and how a figure like Optimus Prime could shift seamlessly from robot to vehicle. I apply that same curiosity to my career: I love diving into the small details and engineering mechanics to ensure they come together to build something sophisticated, adaptable, and impact-driven.

me-2.question: What makes you tick?
me-2.answer: I am driven by the boundless potential of the current technology landscape. We are living in a transformative era where AI is reshaping our daily reality, and that evolution is what excites me. It’s not just about the code; it’s about opening 'new windows' for creativity and utility. What truly makes me tick is the opportunity to bridge the gap between complex technology and real human needs. I am motivated by impact—I want to contribute to this shift, ensuring that the tools we build today genuinely improve the way people experience the world tomorrow.

me-3.question: What are your passions?
me-3.answer: Beyond my obsession with AI and technology, I am a builder at heart. I never stopped playing with LEGO; the sets just evolved from hundreds of pieces to thousands. I believe that you don't stop playing because you grow up, you grow up because you stop playing—so I keep that creative inner child alive by tackling complex builds. I share a similar fascination with Transformers, constantly amazed by the engineering required to make a figure like Optimus Prime detailed and functional in both modes. (Check out the 'Fun' section for a glimpse of my collection!) When I step away from the desk, I play chess for fun, fly my drone and cut the footage into short films, and go hiking. Lately, living in Vancouver has also sparked a growing passion for hiking; the mountains here are impossible to ignore.

me-4.question: How did you get started in tech?
me-4.answer: Like many developers, my spark was lit by video games. Spending hours in the worlds of GTA, Call of Duty, and FIFA made me realize that these experiences weren't magic—they were engineering. I became obsessed with understanding the logic and vision behind the screen. That curiosity transitioned me from player to creator. I started by hacking together basic 2D games to understand the mechanics, which naturally evolved into building complex full-stack web applications. While the technology I use has become more advanced, the core motivation hasn't changed: I love the unique satisfaction of writing code that turns an abstract idea into a tangible experience that others can use and enjoy.

me-5.question: Where do you see yourself in 5 years?
me-5.answer: In five years, I see myself having transitioned from an individual contributor to a technical leader, driving an AI initiative that bridges the gap between research and real-world application. My goal is to be at the helm of a product or platform that creates tangible value for thousands—if not millions—of users. I don't just want to be writing code; I want to be architecting solutions. Whether it's in the realm of accessibility or intelligent systems, I envision myself steering projects where advanced AI meets intuitive design, ensuring that the technology we build creates a measurable, positive ripple effect in people's daily lives.

me-6.question: What's your origin story?
me-6.answer: My defining professional turning point was the opportunity to work as an Undergraduate Research Assistant under Professor Dongwook Yoon. This role was where my career branched out from simply being a student to becoming a true researcher and engineer. It grounded my theoretical interest in AI into rigorous, practical application. Professor Yoon taught me that research is about far more than just publishing papers. He showed me that progress is built on the initiative of taking small, calculated steps for the growth of the community. I learned that while I may not always be the one to 'finish' a massive undertaking, every individual contribution is a vital building block. This philosophy—that significant, impactful solutions are constructed from small, meaningful efforts—now defines my approach to every problem I solve in the industry.

me-easter.question: What's something nobody asks but should?
me-easter.answer: In our fast-paced industry, the most common question is, 'Can you get this done?' But the question I wish people would ask is, 'How do you plan to get this done?' I place immense value on the research and scoping phase of any project. Whether I'm architecting complex internal tooling for an enterprise or tackling a massive LEGO Technic set, I believe the battle is won in the preparation. Thoroughly mapping out project parameters—or simply sorting your bricks before you build—might feel like slowing down initially, but it exponentially speeds up the execution. For me, a smoother, high-quality construction process always beats a rushed start.

pro-1.question: Can I see your resume?
pro-1.answer: Open Resume from the dock or Home to view the updated PDF. I am a software engineer and HCI/AI researcher: a part-time Jr. AI Implementations Engineer at IFS Copperleaf, an undergraduate research assistant at UBC SOCIUS Lab, and a builder of Roadpack, Mune, and BuildStory.

pro-2.question: Why should I hire you?
pro-2.answer: You should hire me because I combine the disciplined mindset of a researcher with the agility of a rapid learner. I treat engineering as a craft—prioritizing thorough scoping and scalable design—but I also possess the adaptability to pick up new tech stacks and pivot quickly as project needs evolve. My background in both academic research and industry co-ops has trained me to handle ambiguity effectively. I don't just solve the problem in front of me; I learn the context around it to ensure the solution fits the team's broader goals. I am ready to hit the ground running, bringing both technical expertise and a hunger to grow.

pro-3.question: What makes you a valuable team member?
pro-3.answer: I believe that great software is built by teams, not just individuals. My greatest strength as a teammate is that I value feedback and constructive criticism over my own ego. I view code reviews and design critiques as essential tools for optimization, not personal attacks. I actively seek out different perspectives to ensure we aren't just building fast, but building right. Whether it's supporting a peer or aligning on a difficult architectural decision, I prioritize open communication to ensure the whole team moves forward together.

pro-4.question: Where are you working now?
pro-4.answer: Since October 2025, my IFS Copperleaf work has progressed from an AI Engineering Co-op to a part-time Jr. AI Implementations Engineer role. I take production AI and data applications from stakeholder discovery to deployment using Databricks, Spark, Delta Lake, and LLM APIs. I owned an ROI Analytics Portal adopted by Department Leaders and Senior Leadership, and built a Data Validation Portal saving an estimated 160+ employee hours annually. I also research HCI/AI at UBC SOCIUS Lab under Professor Dongwook Yoon, since February 2025.

pro-5.question: What's your educational background?
pro-5.answer: I am pursuing a BSc in Computer Science with an AI Specialization and a Commerce Minor at the University of British Columbia, September 2022 to expected graduation in May 2027. My recognition includes the Work Learn International Undergraduate Research Award, Faculty of Science International Student Scholar, and Dean’s Honors List. I also won the Codegen sponsor prize at Hack the North 2024 and first place in the SAP Stream at youCode 2025.

pro-6.question: Tell me about your work philosophy
pro-6.answer: My work philosophy is built on the concept of 'informed iteration.' I don't believe in rushing to a solution without understanding the problem space, but I also don't believe in analysis paralysis. I scope thoroughly, build a strong foundation, and then iterate rapidly based on data and feedback. I believe that good code is readable, scalable, and above all, solves the actual human problem it was intended to address.

proj-1.question: What projects are you most proud of?
proj-1.answer: My recent projects are Roadpack, Mune, and BuildStory. Roadpack is a live App Store app for coordinating trips across vehicles, with a real-time Cloudflare backend. I co-founded Mune, a live App Store personal finance app with on-device AI and production Plaid connectivity. BuildStory is a local-first CLI/TUI that turns Git and AI coding sessions into engineering stories, with an open-source scanner and 330+ automated tests. At UBC, I am first author of Agentic Web Accessibility Auditing and second author of WRAP; both are submitted to ACM CHI 2027.

proj-2.question: Show me something impressive
proj-2.answer: Roadpack and Mune are live on the App Store, and BuildStory has an open-source scanner with 330+ automated tests. My first-author public accessibility preprint evaluates 40 WCAG-specific agents and a shared 31-tool library on 250 page–criterion records across 11 platforms. The agents recovered 67/78 positive cases: 86% recall at 56% precision, compared with 36% axe-core and 67% uncued-VLM recall. Agentic Web Accessibility Auditing and my second-author work WRAP are submitted to ACM CHI 2027.

proj-7.question: Tell me about LLM Pro Max
proj-7.answer: LLM Pro Max won the Codegen sponsor prize at Hack the North 2024. It's a revolutionary codebase analysis platform that intelligently breaks codebases into manageable chunks and feeds only relevant information to LLMs, ensuring token efficiency and improved response accuracy. The system uses advanced RAG techniques including query expansion and re-ranking, leveraging ChromaDB for vector embeddings and Cohere for the chatbot. I built an interactive dependency graph visualization using NetworkX and Pyvis that shows relationships between different parts of the codebase. The platform achieved 86% query relevancy score, significantly improving how developers interact with large codebases. The tech stack includes React.js, Python, FastAPI, ChromaDB, NetworkX, Auth0 for authentication, and Convex for backend and database storage.

proj-8.question: Tell me about Re-Plate
proj-8.answer: Re-Plate won 1st place in the SAP Stream at youCode 2025. I built the entire backend and connected it to the frontend, along with parts of the frontend itself. It's an AI-powered food donation platform that connects surplus food to food-insecure people through intelligent donation matching. The system uses Google Gemini Vision API for automated food classification and combines it with three optimized Machine Learning models (TensorFlow and PyTorch) for image analysis. I built a combined endpoint that joins the team's image models with Gemini text recognition, which reached 100% expiration-date accuracy on our test set. I also built the ApexCharts impact dashboard. The platform features food safety assessment, donation impact tracking (measuring CO₂ emissions offset and waste reduction), and shelter matching. Built with Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Python FastAPI backend, and ApexCharts for analytics visualization. The system addresses the critical problem of 1.3 billion tons of food wasted globally while 828 million people go hungry.

proj-9.question: Tell me about CoviNet
proj-9.answer: CoviNet was my CruzHacks 2022 winning project (QB3 @ UCSC sponsor). It's a comprehensive COVID-19 resource platform built with Flutter that connects users with testing locations, health services, and verified information. The app features real-time messaging using Firebase's real-time database, Google Maps API integration for finding nearby test centers, YouTube API for informational videos, and News API for verified COVID updates. I implemented test report tracking, COVID case alerts by region using synthetic datasets from Gretel, and a messaging system that allows users to connect with others dealing with COVID. The tech stack includes Flutter, Dart, Firebase (Real-time Database), Google Cloud, News-API, and YouTube API. This was one of my first major mobile app projects and taught me a lot about real-time data synchronization and API integration.

proj-10.question: Tell me about the AI Policy Aggregator
proj-10.answer: The AI Policy Aggregator is a production-ready full-stack application I built over five months (February-June 2025) that addresses information overload in AI policy through systematic content curation and personalized summarization. The system aggregates content from four major policy sources (OECD, CAIDP, arXiv, Brookings) using custom scrapers, encodes them into ChromaDB using sentence transformers, and generates personalized weekly briefings. The key innovation is a two-stage anti-hallucination approach: Stage 1 uses semantic filtering with query expansion to narrow 200 retrieved articles to 20-50 highly relevant documents, and Stage 2 enforces strict source attribution through systematic prompt engineering with JSON mode validation. It was deployed on AWS, built with FastAPI backend, React 19 + TypeScript frontend, and Firebase authentication.

proj-3.question: Tell me about your AI/ML projects
proj-3.answer: My AI work spans production enterprise applications at IFS Copperleaf, agentic accessibility research, and on-device models in Mune. The accessibility framework has 40 WCAG-specific agents and a shared 31-tool browser/accessibility library. On 250 page–criterion records across 11 platforms, it achieved 86% recall at 56% precision; findings require human review. In Mune I built the on-device Gemma pipeline and made small models call finance tools reliably. BuildStory normalizes coding-session data from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini Antigravity.

proj-4.question: What's your biggest technical challenge?
proj-4.answer: Roadpack required coordinating shared state across intermittently connected vehicles. Its backend uses Cloudflare Durable Objects and WebSockets for authoritative snapshots, idempotent commands, and offline outboxes, with D1, R2, and queued push delivery. I also don't own a Mac, so every TestFlight and App Store release (1.0.0, 1.0.1 and 1.1.0) ships from Windows through GitHub Actions macOS runners. The hardest part was signing: each run starts with an empty keychain, so automatic signing asked Apple for a new certificate on every build until the account hit Apple's certificate cap. I fixed the cause by importing one existing signing identity from repository secrets into a temporary keychain that is deleted at the end of every job, and by asking the App Store Connect API for the next build number. The app spans 203 Swift files across 13 feature areas, with 40 iOS and 20 backend test files.

proj-5.question: Which project taught you the most?
proj-5.answer: Roadpack taught me the most, because I had to own everything: the native app, a real-time backend, and a release pipeline for an iPhone app I built without owning a Mac. Getting releases out of GitHub Actions meant understanding Apple code signing properly: a fresh runner with an empty keychain kept asking Apple for new certificates until the account hit its cap, so I imported one signing identity into a temporary keychain instead. Earlier, the AI Policy Aggregator taught me that grounded RAG output comes from architecture (filter first, then generate with strict source attribution), not from prompt wording alone.

proj-6.question: What are you building right now?
proj-6.answer: My ongoing work includes Roadpack (since August 2026), BuildStory (since July 2026), and Mune (since May 2026). Roadpack and Mune are live on the App Store; BuildStory’s scanner and report engine are open source, with an optional hosted portal for recaps, receipts, and published chapters. Alongside those products, I work part-time on AI implementations at IFS Copperleaf and research accessibility at UBC SOCIUS Lab. I am first author of Agentic Web Accessibility Auditing and second author of WRAP, both submitted to ACM CHI 2027.

proj-easter.question: What project idea keeps you up at night?
proj-easter.answer: I dream of building the 'Universal LEGO Architect.' Ideally, you would just snap a photo of a random pile of loose bricks, and an AI—powered by object detection and geometric constraint solving—would analyze your exact inventory. It would then generate step-by-step 3D instructions for a brand new model that you can build right now, optimized for the pieces you actually have. It’s the perfect intersection of my technical interests (Computer Vision, Graph Theory) and my personal obsession.

proj-roadpack.question: Tell me about Roadpack and its launch
proj-roadpack.answer: I independently built Roadpack, a native Swift/SwiftUI group-trip app, live on the App Store. It includes live pack locations, stop requests, regrouping, expenses, Rewind, Live Activities, widgets, App Intents, Universal Link/QR invites, and background location. Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, WebSockets, D1, R2, and queued push delivery support authoritative snapshots, idempotent commands, and offline outboxes. It spans 203 Swift files across 13 feature areas, with 40 iOS and 20 backend test files. I release from Windows through GitHub Actions macOS runners: three App Store releases so far (1.0.0, 1.0.1, 1.1.0). Roadpack got its first Pro subscriber within its first six downloads, before I did any marketing. Watch the launch film in Selected Work or visit https://roadpack.app.

proj-paper.question: What is your latest research paper?
proj-paper.answer: I am first author of Agentic Web Accessibility Auditing, a public September 2026 preprint with Pranav Karthik, Byungjun Bae, and Dongwook Yoon. It implements 40 WCAG-specific agents with a shared 31-tool browser/accessibility library. On 250 page–criterion records across 11 platforms, it recovered 67/78 positive cases: 86% recall at 56% precision, against 36% axe-core and 67% uncued-VLM recall. The paper is submitted to ACM CHI 2027. I am also second author of WRAP, which optimizes WCAG task allocation across automated and human audit modalities and is submitted to the same conference. The public preprint is https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09379v2.

proj-buildstory.question: What is BuildStory?
proj-buildstory.answer: BuildStory is my local-first TypeScript/Node.js CLI and TUI, started in July 2026. It converts Git history and AI coding sessions from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini Antigravity into structured engineering stories. Its privacy scanner streams 64 KB JSONL chunks, normalizes provider token/cost data, never reads source-file bodies, and validates canonical uploads with redacted reporting. It has 330+ automated tests. The open-source scanner is at https://github.com/Arjun-Mishra-312/buildstory-scan and the site is https://buildstory.dev.

proj-mune.question: Tell me about Mune and its on-device AI
proj-mune.answer: I co-founded Mune, a personal finance iPhone app started in May 2026 and live on the App Store. It includes Safe-to-Spend, budgets, goals, subscriptions, notifications, and production Plaid bank connectivity. I built the on-device Gemma pipeline on LiteRT-LM and hardened tool calling for small models. Tiny models often describe a tool call in prose instead of making it, so I added a corrective retry, and the assistant answers from finance tool results rather than the model's own arithmetic. Phones under 8 GB default to a 2B model. Pranav and I were both iOS developers on the app. A Node.js/Vercel backend handles Plaid token exchange, webhooks, transaction refresh, authentication, and account lifecycle; RevenueCat supports subscriptions. App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/mune-private-finance-ai/id6777609206.

proj-wrap.question: What is WRAP and your CHI research?
proj-wrap.answer: I am second author of WRAP, which optimizes WCAG task allocation across automated and human audit modalities. WRAP and my first-author Agentic Web Accessibility Auditing paper are both submitted to ACM CHI 2027. Agentic Web Accessibility Auditing also has a public preprint; neither submission is described as accepted.

skill-1.question: What are your skills?
skill-1.answer: My languages include Swift, TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, C/C++, SQL, Java, and Dart. I build native apps with SwiftUI and the iOS SDK; web products with React/Next.js; and systems with Node.js, FastAPI, Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, WebSockets, D1, R2, Databricks, Spark, and Delta Lake. My AI work includes LLM agents, MCP, RAG, VLMs, LangChain, OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, PyTorch, MLX Swift, and LLM evaluation. I also use Flutter, Playwright, GitHub Actions, and Docker.

skill-2.question: What's your tech stack?
skill-2.answer: Roadpack uses Swift/SwiftUI, MapKit, Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, WebSockets, D1, and R2. BuildStory uses TypeScript, Node.js, a CLI/TUI, Git, JSONL, and LLM APIs. Mune uses Swift, MLX Swift, LiteRT-LM, Node.js/Vercel, Plaid, and RevenueCat. At IFS Copperleaf, I work with Databricks, Spark, Delta Lake, and LLM APIs.

skill-3.question: What technologies do you work with?
skill-3.answer: Swift, TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, C/C++, SQL, Java, Dart, SwiftUI, iOS SDK, React, Next.js, Flutter, Node.js, FastAPI, Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, WebSockets, D1, R2, Databricks, Spark, Delta Lake, Playwright, GitHub Actions, Docker, LLM agents, MCP, RAG, VLMs, LangChain, OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, PyTorch, MLX Swift, and LLM evaluation.

skill-4.question: What's your favorite programming language?
skill-4.answer: Python is my undisputed favorite. It is the lingua franca of AI, and its ecosystem allows me to go from a scrappy idea to a working prototype faster than anything else. Whether I'm scripting a quick automation or training a multimodal transformer, Python just gets out of the way and lets me build. That said, I have a healthy respect for C++. My time teaching systems programming taught me that when you really need to manage memory or optimize performance down to the metal, nothing beats it.

skill-5.question: What are you learning right now?
skill-5.answer: My current work develops agentic accessibility systems, on-device LLMs with MLX Swift and LiteRT-LM, real-time distributed systems for Roadpack, and privacy-aware developer tooling in BuildStory. I also take production AI/data applications from stakeholder discovery through deployment at IFS Copperleaf.

skill-6.question: Frontend or backend?
skill-6.answer: I build across the product: native iOS interfaces, web applications, backend systems, and data/AI infrastructure. Roadpack connects a SwiftUI client to real-time Cloudflare trip rooms; Mune combines a native finance app, local models, and Plaid integration; and my Copperleaf work takes enterprise AI applications end-to-end.

skill-easter.question: What skill do you secretly want to learn?
skill-easter.answer: I’ve been eyeing Rust for a while now. Given my background in C++ and systems programming, I’m fascinated by the promise of memory safety without a garbage collector. It feels like the natural evolution for high-performance engineering—getting that low-level control I love, but with a compiler that actually stops me from shooting myself in the foot before I even run the code!

fun-2.question: What's the craziest thing you've ever done?
fun-2.answer: For a self-proclaimed foodie who rarely hit the gym, blindly saying 'yes' to a 'medium' hike with friends was definitely the craziest decision I’ve made. What started as a casual plan turned into a 12km+ odyssey. We surprisingly had to climb over 350m of elevation just to reach the start of the trail, followed by another 533m to the peak. There were moments where I genuinely contemplated just sitting down on the trail and living there. But pushed by my friends and a perfect Vancouver summer day, I made it to the top. The view was absolutely worth it (check out the photo!), instantly washing away the exhaustion... at least until the journey back down reminded my legs exactly what I had just put them through.

fun-3.question: Tell me something fun about you
fun-3.answer: I organize my LEGO pieces by color and then by shape before I start building. It drives my friends crazy because it takes hours, but I swear it's the only efficient way to build a 4,000-piece set without losing your mind.

fun-4.question: What are your hobbies?
fun-4.answer: I’m a collector and a builder. I spend a lot of my free time building complex LEGO Technic sets and collecting Transformers figures—I'm still amazed by the engineering behind the transformation mechanics. I also play Chess. I'm moderately good with just a few specific openings, but I play enthusiastically! And as mentioned, I've recently started exploring Vancouver's hiking trails to disconnect from the screen.

fun-5.question: Got any adventure stories?
fun-5.answer: Aside from surviving the mountains of Vancouver, my biggest adventures usually happen in the code editor at 3 AM. But seriously, navigating life as an international student is an adventure in itself—learning a new culture, navigating a new city, and building a life from scratch.

fun-6.question: Mac or PC?
fun-6.answer: I am a PC guy at heart because I need the raw GPU power for training models and the flexibility to upgrade hardware. That said, I appreciate the Mac ecosystem for its Unix-based terminal and battery life when I'm coding on the go. But if I had to pick one island to live on? PC.

fun-7.question: Coffee or tea?
fun-7.answer: Being from India, the answer has to be Tea—or as we call it, Chai. (And strictly just 'Chai', never 'Chai Tea'!). It is my mandatory morning wake-up and the fuel that keeps my day running. It’s also my go-to companion for those late-night coding sessions whenever I need an extra push.

fun-easter.question: What's your most embarrassing tech moment?
fun-easter.answer: I once spent hours debugging an Amazon Alexa project that absolutely refused to connect to the university Wi-Fi. I tore apart the codebase looking for the bug. Eventually, I took a step back, read the network documentation, and realized I simply had to whitelist the device's MAC address on the portal. I was frantically searching for the light switch inside the room with every means possible, only to realize that in this case, the switch was actually outside the room.

contact-1.question: How can I reach you?
contact-1.answer: The best way to reach me is via LinkedIn or Email. I’m always open to discussing new opportunities, AI research, or just geeking out over the latest LLM benchmarks. You can also check out my code on GitHub.

contact-2.question: Let's work together!
contact-2.answer: I am always looking for interesting problems to solve. Whether you are a startup looking for an AI engineer, a researcher needing a collaborator on multimodal models, or a fellow student with a hackathon idea, I’d love to hear from you.

contact-3.question: What kind of project would make you say 'yes' immediately?
contact-3.answer: I say 'yes' to projects that have a clear human impact. If you are building something that uses technology to make the world more accessible, inclusive, or efficient, I am in. I’m particularly drawn to challenges that require a mix of research (figuring out how) and engineering (making it scale).

contact-4.question: Where are you located?
contact-4.answer: I am currently based in Vancouver, British Columbia, completing my degree at UBC. I love the tech scene here, but I am accustomed to working in distributed teams.

contact-5.question: Are you open to opportunities?
contact-5.answer: Yes! I graduate from UBC in May 2027 and I'm looking for new-grad roles: software engineering, forward-deployed engineering, and AI engineering. I'm also happy to talk about iOS roles. Reach me by email or LinkedIn.

contact-6.question: What's your ideal next role?
contact-6.answer: I am looking for a role as an AI Engineer or Full-Stack Developer where I can get my hands dirty with production-level code. Ideally, I want to join a team that values engineering rigor but isn't afraid to experiment with bleeding-edge AI technologies.

contact-easter.question: What would make you relocate?
contact-easter.answer: A challenging problem, a brilliant team, and... good Chai. If you have those three, I can pack my bags.

surprise-me.question: Surprise me!
surprise-me.answer: Did you know that the LEGO brick design hasn't changed since 1958? A brick from today still fits perfectly with one from 60 years ago. That is the kind of backward compatibility I strive for in my code.

tell-me-a-secret.question: Tell me a secret
tell-me-a-secret.answer: I treat Large Language Models like colleagues. I find myself saying 'please' and 'thank you' in my prompts, and I’m secretly convinced it makes the code output better. Call it superstition, but if the AI uprising ever happens, I want to be on their good side.
